n: This begins Jeremiah’s famous “Temple Sermon,” probably given early in Jehoiakim’s reign (about 609 BC). Jeremiah 26 tells how it nearly got him killed.

f.w: The word that came to Jeremiah

n: God sends Jeremiah to stand at the temple gate and speak to worshippers as they enter—the most public and provocative place possible.

f.w: Stand in the gate of the LORD's house

n: The message: change your ways and actions, and I will let you keep living in this land.

f.w: Amend your ways and your doings

n: Don’t trust the deceptive chant, “This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord!” People assumed that because God’s house stood in Jerusalem, the city could never fall—no matter how they lived.

f.g: Repeated three times as a kind of magic slogan for safety.

f.w: Trust ye not in lying words

n: If you truly change your ways and deal justly with one another…
…if you don’t oppress foreigners, orphans, and widows, don’t shed innocent blood, and don’t chase other gods to your own harm…

f.w: the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow

n: …then I will let you live in this land forever. The promise is conditional on covenant faithfulness.
But you trust in lies that won’t help you.
You steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods—breaking most of the Ten Commandments…

f.w: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery

n: …and then come stand in My house and say, “We’re safe!”—only to go on doing these detestable things? Worship cannot be a license to sin.

f.g: We are safe—as if the temple were a hiding place.

n: Has My house become a hideout for robbers? Jesus quoted this when He drove the moneychangers out of the temple. Robbers return to their den to be safe between crimes.
Go look at Shiloh, where My tabernacle once stood, and see what I did to it. Shiloh had been Israel’s worship center, but it was destroyed, likely by the Philistines.

f.g: A town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood in the days of Eli and Samuel.

n: God “rose up early” to speak to them—an idiom for persistent, eager effort—but they wouldn’t listen or answer.

f.g: A Jeremiah idiom: speaking again and again, with eagerness.

n: So God will do to this temple what He did to Shiloh. Babylon destroyed Solomon’s temple in 586 BC.

f.w: as I have done to Shiloh

n: He will cast them out of His sight just as He cast out Ephraim—the northern kingdom, exiled by Assyria in 722 BC.
A startling command: don’t pray for this people—I won’t listen. Their rebellion has reached a point where intercession can’t stop the judgment.

f.w: pray not thou for this people

n: Don’t you see what they’re doing everywhere in Judah and Jerusalem?
Whole families join in: children gather wood, fathers light fires, women knead dough for cakes to the “queen of heaven”—probably the goddess Ishtar/Astarte. Idolatry had become a family tradition.

f.g: Likely the Mesopotamian Ishtar or Canaanite Astarte, goddess of love and fertility.
Wine or other liquid poured out as an offering.

n: Are they really hurting Me? No—they’re hurting themselves, to their own shame.

f.w: the confusion of their own faces

n: God’s anger will pour out on people, animals, trees, and crops, burning without being put out.
Sarcastically God says: go ahead, add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves—they mean nothing to Me.

f.w: Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices
f.g: Burnt offerings were wholly burned for God; God says eat them too—they’re no longer holy to Him.

n: When God brought Israel out of Egypt, His first concern wasn’t sacrifices. Sacrifices weren’t the heart of the covenant.
What He commanded was: obey My voice, and I will be your God and you will be My people. Obedience is the core of covenant relationship.

f.w: Obey my voice, and I will be your God

n: But they didn’t listen; they followed their own stubborn hearts and went backward instead of forward.
Since the Exodus, God sent prophet after prophet, day after day.
Yet they didn’t listen; they stiffened their necks and did worse than their ancestors.

f.g: Were stubborn, like an ox refusing the yoke.

n: God tells Jeremiah plainly: you will speak, but they won’t listen; you will call, but they won’t answer. Faithful prophets aren’t measured by how many listen.

f.w: they will not hearken to thee

n: Say: this nation won’t obey God or accept correction. Truth has died; it has vanished from their lips.
Cut off your hair and throw it away—a sign of mourning—and wail on the bare hills, for the Lord has rejected this generation.

f.g: Shaving the head was a sign of deep mourning.

n: They even put their idols in God’s own temple, defiling it.

f.w: they have set their abominations in the house

n: Worst of all, they built shrines at Tophet in the Valley of Hinnom to burn their children—something God never commanded and never even thought of. God is horrified by it.

f.g: A place of child sacrifice in the Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem.

f.w: the valley of the son of Hinnom
f.g: Hebrew Ge-Hinnom—the origin of “Gehenna,” a New Testament word for hell.

f.w: neither came it into my heart

n: That valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter; so many will die that they’ll bury people there until there’s no room left.
Bodies will be left as food for birds and beasts, with no one to scare them away—one of the covenant curses.

f.w: meat for the fowls of the heaven

n: God will silence every sound of joy—celebration, gladness, and the voices of bride and groom at weddings. The land will be desolate. Later Jeremiah promises these sounds will return.

f.w: the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride
